findings.gap: The cyan kicker gives location and process posture, but it does not provide the required one-line position or clearly state what Kennedy does.
The first supporting paragraph is set nearly as a subheadline, spans four prominent lines, and competes with the display name instead of behaving as plain-spoken supporting prose.
The oversized paragraph consumes too much of the opening screen and creates a loose, billboard-like text block rather than the bar's dense-but-never-cramped editorial rhythm.
Copy about fragments being gated, rendered, and watched turns the person into a demonstration of a system; this reads closer to product-proof landing copy than a personal introduction.
Electric cyan is confined to a small eyebrow while the largest non-display text uses muted beige, so the cyan counterweight is too weak to structure the composition.
The large sans-serif prose has a heavy, display-like presence and weakens the intended contrast between one editorial serif display and restrained plain-text prose.
The supposed position line is an abstract slogan rather than a concrete role, and it wraps to two lines in the shown viewport, missing the requirement for one line of position.
The large cyan slogan occupies nearly as much visual territory as the name and becomes a competing headline, though the hierarchy remains cleaner than Candidate A.
“Systems that hold a standard” is polished but broad enough to serve a consultancy or software product; it does not identify a distinctive personal practice without relying on the paragraph below.
The final status line is small and visually detached, reading like auxiliary metadata rather than part of a deliberately paced editorial paragraph sequence.

findings.gap: The filled surface and border create exactly the card-like framing named as the anti-reference; the person is presented as a boxed product component instead of a well-set editorial page.

The abstract automation thesis and closing line "That is what this is" read like product-positioning copy; they reveal little concrete or personal about Kennedy and could sit on a generic AI tooling landing page.
The required one-line position wraps across two lines, and its aphoristic wording is a tagline rather than a clear statement of what Kennedy does.
Electric cyan owns the largest and most forceful colored text, reversing the specified relationship in which molten amber is primary and cyan is only the counterweight.
"Control systems · interfaces · evidence over argument" is a keyword strapline, not a grammatical one-line position, which pushes the hero toward portfolio-product taxonomy.
The warm dark and amber primary are on-direction, but the composition contains no visible electric-cyan counterweight, leaving the palette less distinctive than the seven-role contract.
The inset panel compresses all content into a shallow bounded rectangle with uniform padding; it feels like a dashboard card rather than editorial rhythm distributed across the opening screen.
The "Currently" line drops to a small, low-contrast footnote while being one of only two supporting paragraphs, making the lower end of the hierarchy feel prematurely diminished.

The bright amber sans-serif strapline has the familiar visual grammar of a SaaS subheading; it does not exploit the editorial display/plain-text contrast with the restraint of the reference direction.
Although Candidate A becomes specific and personal in its supporting copy, the lead claim is still a polished standards-oriented slogan that could headline many infrastructure or governance products.
Uses bg-surface and border-border framing, directly violating the explicit anti-reference that a card is a component and not a person.
The card layout makes the section read like a stock SaaS product landing page rather than an editorial personal site.
Including a third paragraph risks making the hero read like an about page, even if technically split between position and supporting text.
